questions.q: Propan-1-ol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO₃ in dilute H₂SO₄, added to an acetone solution). The product is:
questions.explain: In the aqueous acidic Jones conditions the aldehyde formed first is hydrated and oxidised again, so a 1° alcohol gives the carboxylic acid. Stopping at propanal needs an anhydrous reagent such as PCC.

questions.q: Why does Jones oxidation of a saturated primary alcohol not stop at the aldehyde?
options: The aldehyde forms a hydrate R–CH(OH)₂ in water, which is itself an alcohol and is oxidised to R–COOH
Acetone oxidises the aldehyde to the acid
Cr(III) formed in the reaction oxidises aldehydes
H₂SO₄ alone converts aldehydes into carboxylic acids
questions.explain: The hydrate forms a new chromate ester and is oxidised again. Allylic and benzylic aldehydes hydrate only slightly, so those 1° alcohols usually stop at the aldehyde.

questions.q: But-3-en-2-ol, CH₂=CH–CH(OH)–CH₃, is oxidised with Jones reagent. The product is:
questions.explain: Jones reagent oxidises the 2° alcohol to a ketone and generally leaves the C=C intact, giving the enone CH₂=CH–CO–CH₃.

questions.q: In the balanced Jones oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone, how many moles of CrO₃ are consumed for every 3 mol of alcohol?
questions.explain: 3R₂CHOH + 2CrO₃ + 3H₂SO₄ → 3R₂C=O + Cr₂(SO₄)₃ + 6H₂O. Each Cr(VI) → Cr(III) gains 3 electrons while each alcohol loses 2, so 3 alcohol molecules need 2 CrO₃.
